title: Welcome
notes: This project investigates whether principles of graphic design can be represented computationally. Rather than generating graphics with machine learning, the objective was to analyse existing compositions and make design decisions measurable.

title: Composition Analysis Model
notes: The project explores whether established compositional principles can be translated into objective rules that a machine learning system can identify and evaluate.

title: Concept
notes: The research began with an interest in understanding whether visual composition could be analysed computationally. If compositional relationships can be measured consistently, they may become easier to teach and study.

title: Objective
notes: The objective was to detect graphical elements within a composition before analysing their positional and proportional relationships against established design principles.

title: Principles
notes: To keep the project achievable, the research focused on two principles that could be represented mathematically and therefore translated into computational logic.

title: Rule of Thirds
notes: The Rule of Thirds was selected because it defines clear positional relationships, making it well suited to algorithmic comparison.

title: Canvas
notes: The first stage was defining the composition boundary that all positional measurements would reference.

title: 3×3 Grid
notes: Dividing the canvas into a regular grid transforms an abstract design principle into measurable coordinates.

title: Focal Points
notes: These intersection points provide reference locations where visual attention is commonly directed.

title: Attention Distribution
notes: The percentages illustrate approximate visual weighting across the composition, providing a basis for comparison rather than strict rules.

title: Element Placement
notes: Detected elements could later be compared against these intersections to determine whether they align with the Rule of Thirds.

title: Rows
notes: The same grid can also be interpreted horizontally to evaluate broader structural alignment.

title: Columns
notes: Column alignment provides another measurable interpretation of the same compositional framework.

title: Examples
notes: Professional examples were collected to understand how consistently these principles appear in existing graphic design.

title: Golden Ratio
notes: Unlike the Rule of Thirds, the Golden Ratio focuses on proportional relationships and visual hierarchy rather than position.

title: Golden Ratio Diagram
notes: The geometric construction provides a mathematical framework that can potentially be measured computationally.

title: Mathematical Representation
notes: Understanding the mathematical relationship was necessary before considering how it could be translated into software.

title: Visual Hierarchy
notes: The Golden Ratio can be interpreted as a way of comparing the relative importance of visual elements.

title: Hierarchy
notes: Rather than measuring placement, this stage considers proportional relationships between detected elements.

title: Typography Example
notes: Typography provides a straightforward demonstration of proportional hierarchy in practice.

title: Application
notes: With the principles defined, the next stage was identifying an appropriate machine learning approach.

title: Template Selection
notes: Object detection was chosen because compositional analysis first requires an understanding of what visual elements are present.

title: Object Detection
notes: Bounding boxes provide a simplified representation of graphical elements that can later be analysed mathematically.

title: Dataset Selection
notes: The chosen dataset needed consistent layouts, recognisable elements and similar aspect ratios to support meaningful comparisons.

title: Car Posters
notes: Car posters satisfied these requirements through repeated visual structures while still offering compositional variety.

title: Example Poster
notes: A single poster was used to demonstrate the proposed analytical workflow.

title: Bounding Boxes
notes: Each detected object is simplified into a geometric boundary for later analysis.

title: Centre Points
notes: The centre point of each bounding box provides a consistent positional reference.

title: Overlay
notes: A Rule of Thirds grid can then be overlaid directly onto the composition.

title: Initial Comparison
notes: The relationship between detected centre points and grid lines becomes computationally measurable.

title: Limitation
notes: A direct point-to-line comparison proved too strict to be practically useful.

title: Tolerance
notes: Increasing the width of the guide lines introduced tolerance into the analysis, making the system more reliable.

title: Row and Column Detection
notes: Bounding boxes could also be analysed against rows and columns, extending the Rule of Thirds beyond intersection points.

title: Golden Ratio Extension
notes: The same detected elements could later support proportional analysis using the Golden Ratio.

title: Detection Accuracy
notes: Object detection accuracy became a significant limitation because compositional measurements depend entirely on reliable detection.

title: Case Study
notes: A single element was isolated to investigate how inaccuracies influence the analytical process.

title: Standard Detection
notes: Traditional object detection produces bounding boxes based on physical boundaries rather than perceived visual importance.

title: Bounding Box Accuracy
notes: Although technically correct, the detected boundary does not necessarily represent the visual weight of the object.

title: Perceived Size
notes: Visual importance depends on more than physical dimensions, introducing another variable into the analysis.

title: Average Colour
notes: Average colour was explored as a reference point for measuring visual contrast.

title: Contrast
notes: This led to the idea that contrast may provide a better representation of visual significance than object size alone.

title: Alternative Approach
notes: An alternative method was proposed that measures only the visually dominant regions of each detected object.

title: Photoshop Prototype
notes: The concept was validated manually before considering automation.

title: Practical Decision
notes: Given the project timeframe, the simpler bounding box approach was retained for the working prototype.

title: Validation
notes: Additional examples demonstrated that conventional object detection remained sufficiently accurate for proof-of-concept testing.

title: Training
notes: The next stage focused on producing a custom object detection model.

title: Dataset Collection
notes: Training images were collected to maximise visual consistency while maintaining compositional variation.

title: Image Selection
notes: A relatively small but carefully selected dataset was assembled for the prototype.

title: Annotation
notes: Roboflow accelerated the annotation process while maintaining consistent labels.

title: Data Augmentation
notes: Image augmentation improved dataset diversity without altering the underlying compositions.

title: Export
notes: The completed dataset was transferred into Create ML for training.

title: Model Training
notes: Training continued until improvements became marginal relative to computation time.

title: Initial Testing
notes: The resulting model produced sufficiently accurate detections for compositional experimentation.

title: Deployment
notes: Attention shifted from model performance towards how the analysis could be experienced by users.

title: Initial App
notes: The first deployment demonstrated successful object detection but limited compositional analysis.

title: Grid Alignment
notes: The analytical overlay was corrected so it referenced the image rather than the display.

title: Improved Visualisation
notes: Aligning the guides with the image made compositional relationships easier to interpret.

title: Row Detection
notes: The revised interface made row alignment immediately visible.

title: Grid Detection
notes: Grid-line relationships also became significantly clearer.

title: Reflection
notes: The prototype demonstrated that established compositional principles could be visualised computationally.

title: Refinement
notes: Interface improvements focused on improving clarity rather than adding functionality.

title: Analysis Interface
notes: Visual feedback was refined to better communicate the underlying analysis.

title: Row Logic
notes: Additional logic was introduced to detect elements fully contained within rows or columns.

title: Thresholding
notes: Simple thresholds reduced false positives by considering the relative size of detected elements.

title: Final Prototype
notes: The completed prototype demonstrated the intended workflow on previously unseen data.

title: Golden Ratio Future Work
notes: Proportional analysis remained unfinished but the underlying detection pipeline was already capable of supporting it.

title: Real-World Deployment
notes: The long-term objective was analysing real posters captured with a mobile device rather than curated images.

title: Next Steps
notes: Future work would expand the range of detectable elements, improve dataset quality and transition from descriptive analysis towards computational design assistance.

title: Ethics
notes: The intention was never to automate graphic design. The project investigates whether computational analysis can make established design principles more transparent and accessible while preserving creative judgement.

title: Conclusion
notes: This project established the technical and conceptual foundations for later research into computational approaches to graphic design education and analysis.
